HEADLINE: Shipton to go, ASIC shake-up looms
TEXT:
Australian Securities and Investments Commission chairman James Shipton will be replaced despite being cleared of any wrongdoing because Treasurer Josh Frydenberg wants a fresh face to overhaul the troubled regulator.

Mr Shipton, who stood aside in October pending an independent investigation into some of his relocation expenses, will return to work on Monday but depart once a replacement is found.

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority deputy chair, John Lonsdale, is one name being kicked around in corporate circles as a possible replacement for Mr Shipton. Acting chair Karen Chester is unlikely to be chosen, sources said, after pushing her credentials for the job hard.

After being cleared, sources said Mr Shipton played hardball with Mr Frydenberg, who had no power to dismiss him. Mr Shipton agreed to depart in return for receiving about $200,000 in salary he was owed since standing down in October.

His former deputy Daniel Crennan, who was also cleared of wrongdoing over his relocation expenses, quit last year.

Both men are said to be glad to be gone.

Labor said the "incompetent" treatment of both men, as well as the departure of Australia Post boss Christine Holgate, who also did nothing wrong, would make it difficult for the government to attract high-calibre people from the private sector.

"It's monumental incompetence," said shadow assistant treasurer Stephen Jones.

"[Mr Frydenberg] and Scott Morrison have destroyed trust with corporate Australia over their handling of both Mr Shipton's case and their confected outrage at waste by senior executives at Australia Post."

It was Labor that first complained about Australia Post.

Mr Frydenberg wants to shake up ASIC and Mr Shipton will help initiate the reform process before he leaves in about three months.

Mr Shipton and Mr Crennan were recruited to sharpen up the regulator following searing criticism from the Hayne royal commission into the banking sector.

Mr Shipton stood aside last year when the federal Auditor-General raised questions about payments of more than $118,000 made by ASIC to KPMG for tax advice he received.

KPMG had reconciled his tax affairs as part of his joining the regulator.

The Auditor-General had also questioned a $750-a-week relocation payment made over two years to Mr Crennan, the former head of enforcement and deputy chairman, totalling almost $70,000.

Auditor-General Grant Hehir said the payments might have exceeded limits set by the remuneration tribunal, which sets pay for public sector workers, and he was also worried that the payments to KPMG did not follow procurement guidelines.

But an independent report into the expenses matter by former inspector-general of intelligence Vivienne Thom cleared Mr Shipton and Mr Crennan of any wrongdoing.

"Dr Thom made no adverse findings regarding Mr Shipton and Mr Crennan,' Mr Frydenberg said.

However, Dr Thom's inquiry was very critical of the current state of the regulator and its processes, including poor governance, concerns over proper use and management of public resources, and a lack of cooperation between ASIC officials.

Hostilities were exposed in October last year when Ms Chester told a Senate committee that Mr Shipton did not tell senior colleagues for more than a year about the Auditor-General's concerns. The matter was raised by the auditor at a "very high level" with the sole "Accountable Authority" - who is Mr Shipton as the head of ASIC - and "it does raise issues of disclosure to the commission at that time of the detail last year".

Dr Thom did suggest that Treasury, which oversees ASIC, seek legal advice as to whether Mr Shipton had breached any codes of conduct regarding conflict of interest covering the regulator or Australian Public Service employees.

Again, there were no adverse findings. "After considering Dr Thom's report and supplementary legal advice provided to the Treasury, concerning these matters, I am satisfied that there have been no instances of misconduct by Mr Shipton," Mr Frydenberg said.

However, Treasury was told to improve the clarity of its employment procedures, such as having clearly defined employment contracts for hiring statutory officers.

"In response, the secretary of the Treasury had moved to implement a new system immediately," Mr Frydenberg said.

Mr Shipton said he was "pleased and unsurprised that the review process has cleared me of any wrongdoing".

"I look forward to returning to my role as ASIC chair and working with the government to reform the corporate regulator," he said.

"I am very appreciative of the confidence Treasurer Frydenberg and the government has placed in me to start the process of strengthening ASIC and transitioning to a new ASIC chair later this year."

Mr Crennan said he too was "pleased that the Treasurer has today announced that Dr Thom's independent report made no adverse findings about me".

"The conclusions were consistent with my expectations at the outset of the review process," he said.

"I will continue to contribute to the financial system in a private capacity as a consultant to the private and public sectors."

Despite being cleared, both men have repaid the money and will receive no severance payment.

The tumult continues a tough run for ASIC, which also included a Federal Court loss in June when the judge dismissed its "wagyu and shiraz" responsible lending case against Westpac and ordered it to pay the bank's costs.

Mr Frydenberg now wants to torpedo the regulations regarding responsible lending.

Shipton's messy exit signals big changes at ASIC
TEXT:
Former inspector-general of intelligence Vivienne Thom made "no adverse findings" against the now-outgoing corporate watchdog chairman James Shipton, but the messy process of his departure portends an imminent wave of change at the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

After standing aside from the role in October, it quickly became clear Shipton would be unable to return on a permanent basis, regardless of any or findings of misconduct, or lack thereof.

And with several months before a new chair is appointed, ASIC employees face a period of uncertainty, particularly after tensions between the top commissioners were so thoroughly aired during the process.

Only days after the Australian National Audit Office raised its concerns about the large expenses claims (which have since been repaid) with Josh Frydenberg in October, acting chairwoman Karen Chester revealed to Parliament that Shipton did not tell senior colleagues for more than a year that the Auditor-General had raised concerns about the housing allowance of almost $70,000 paid to former enforcement boss Daniel Crennan, who resigned in October.

Chester also said the full leadership commission at ASIC was not aware of Shipton's $118,557 KPMG tax services bill that was paid for by ASIC in 2018 until after the ANAO expressed concern in September this year.

One major problem was the auditor raised the issue with the "Accountable Authority" at ASIC, which was Shipton himself. The lack of a governing board above the commissioner level is likely to be rectified.

Not a month passed before Chester then revealed in November that Shipton had opposed a key governance recommendation from a landmark capability review of ASIC, which she had authored in 2015, which sought the creation of a chief executive role.

Shipton and other commissioners had over-ruled the appointment, Chester said, noting she had discussed the recommendation when she first arrived at ASIC under the impression the internal governance model would be adopted.

Shipton, a former Goldman Sachs investment banker turned-regulator turned-Harvard academic was well-liked by his colleagues but faced criticism at the commission for being indecisive, according to multiple ASIC sources. "He had a tendency for dithering," said one.

Chester easily filled the vacuum left by Shipton and Crennan, and sought to shore up confidence in ASIC, quickly appointing Melbourne-based Pitt Group to provide assurance advice over its corporate expenses and to help develop an "audit reporting tool".

She also took legal advice over a short-lived but controversial new role taken by Crennan less than two weeks after his departure at colourful stockbroker EverBlu Capital.

Relations with Canberra, which had been damaged during the Westpac "Wagyu and Shiraz" appeal, were also calmed when Chester sought to relegate the regulator's appeal for more powers to "the past" and pledged to "get on with it".

Chester even reshuffled the deck chairs, realigning the responsibilities of fellow commissioners Sean Hughes, Cathie Armour and Danielle Press, not bothering to wait for the outcome of the review into Shipton.

"Most would agree she is a much more effective leader," says one insider. "It'll certainly be interesting on Monday," one ASIC source said about discussions at upcoming commissioner-level meetings.

Shipton faced criticism for being indecisive, according to ASIC sources.

HEADLINE: Bowen brushes off Fitzgibbon taunts
TEXT:
Labor's new climate spokesman, Chris Bowen, says he has rejected calls from his Right faction colleague Joel Fitzgibbon for the opposition to adopt Coalition emissions policies, promising an economic transition worthy of Bob Hawke and Paul Keating.

Mr Fitzgibbon, who quit Labor's frontbench in November to agitate on energy, this week forced the ouster of Mark Butler from the shadow climate portfolio in a messy reshuffle announced on Thursday by Opposition Leader Anthony Albanese.

The senior NSW Right faction figure believes Labor will lose the next election unless it adopts a more centrist policy, recognising the role gas and coal will continue to play until major shifts to renewables take place in Australia.

Mr Bowen has been charged with better articulating the employment benefits of a clean energy future, in a bid to head off the Coalition's attacks.

He said Mr Fitzgibbon's calls were wrong, and Labor could do better than the government.

"I think that the government's approach is one which is destroying jobs, avoiding the opportunity to create jobs for our kids, good jobs in new industries in growing industries, and to ensure a sustainable and clear energy supply for manufacturing and traditional industries," Mr Bowen told ABC radio.

"That is the key to climate change and energy policy, that's what I'll be focusing on like a laser, and I'll be holding the government to account.

"I believe climate change is the key economic challenge for the nation, and of course for the world. That's what Labor does best, managing economic transitions. That's what Hawke and Keating did."

In a further sign of tension, Mr Fitzgibbon said Mr Bowen still had "his training wheels on".

"I think Chris will come to learn that the reason we've got a fall-off in investment in energy generation is that we can't get more renewables into the system until we get more firming power into the system.

"That means ... one or two new gas-fired generators. That's the important thing he needs to come to understand."

Frontbencher Penny Wong dismissed possible claims to the leadership by former leader Bill Shorten or former deputy leader Tanya Plibersek, potential contenders to replace Mr Albanese before the next election.

"We had six years with Bill and Tanya. Regrettably, we lost both elections," she said on Friday. "We are now looking to the next election, and this reshuffle is all about that.

"We've been very, very clear about our policy direction, and we'll have more to say, as the year progresses, about that."
